strengths: Addresses a practical and underexplored problem: font-controllable text editing guided by an arbitrary user-provided glyph patch, rather than a closed font library or text-only prompt, which has clear utility in professional design workflows.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning an in-house poster benchmark, the public AnyText benchmark (English/Chinese), and handwritten text benchmarks (IAM, CVL), with consistent improvements over multiple strong commercial (Nano Banana, Seedream 4.0, FLUX-Kontext-Pro, Qwen-Image-Edit) and open-source (FLUX-Text, AnyText2, TextCtrl) baselines.

The dual-stream conditioning idea (content reference poster + rendered glyph reference map, injected via a frozen VAE encoder and sequence concatenation) is simple, avoids extra trainable modules like ControlNet, and is shown to be effective via ablation.

The content-style decoupled data curation pipeline, using VLM-based OCR plus LLM-generated disjoint replacement text and DINOv2-based verification, is a sensible engineering solution to a genuine problem (content/style entanglement in training pairs) for real-world (non-synthetic) poster data.
Good coverage of ablations (font style reference on/off, loss weight λ sweep) that clarify design choices and trade-offs (e.g., FSR improving style fidelity at some cost to OCR-measured accuracy).
Distillation for 8-step inference (DMD2) is a useful practical addition demonstrating deployment feasibility without extensively sacrificing quality (though this claim is only lightly substantiated).
weaknesses: Technical novelty is incremental: the core mechanism is LoRA fine-tuning of an existing large editing model (Qwen-Image-Edit) with straightforward sequence-dimension concatenation of VAE-encoded reference/glyph images; there is limited architectural or algorithmic innovation beyond a data pipeline and a weighted loss.

The primary quantitative benchmark ("SkyReels-Text Benchmark", 200 samples) is self-curated and not established in the community, and there is no indication that it or the 100k training dataset will be released, which limits independent verification of the strong reported gains and creates a risk of bias favoring the proposed method.

The data generation pipeline used to build training pairs itself relies on "editing models" to synthesize style-preserving content replacements, verified via DINOv2 similarity — the same DINO metric is later used as an evaluation metric for font style adherence, raising a circularity concern that could inflate DINO-based results.

No user study or perceptual/human evaluation is included despite the central claim being about subjective typographic/style fidelity, which automated metrics (DINO similarity, PSNR, FID) only partially capture.

Ablation in Table 4 shows removing the font style reference (FSR) actually improves Sen. Acc and NED, and the explanation (OCR failing on stylized text, implicit spatial cues) is plausible but not empirically isolated or verified, leaving the trade-off underexplained.

Method and paper provide limited detail on the OCR VLM training data/labels, the exact inpainting/editing model used to generate Xref during training data construction, and possible failure modes (e.g., very small text, extreme font distortions, multi-line paragraph edits) — no explicit limitations or failure-case discussion is presented.
Minor writing/typo issues (e.g., "handwrittent", "optimzer", inconsistent citation numbering for Seedream 4.0 as [31]/[32]) suggest limited proofreading.

Reproducibility is weak: no code, model, or benchmark release is mentioned, and key training details (e.g., exact editing model used for pair generation, full data filtering thresholds) are not fully specified.

strengths: Addresses a clear, practically motivated problem: font-controllable, multi-region text editing for professional poster design, with a user workflow that avoids per-font fine-tuning or font labels.

The dual-stream conditioning design (reference-poster latent + glyph-map latent concatenated with noisy latent) is simple to implement on top of an existing DiT editing backbone and avoids adding new trainable modules such as ControlNet branches.

The data curation pipeline, including VLM-based OCR for ornamental/calligraphic text and a content-style decoupling verification step (OCR for content, DINOv2 for style), is a reasonable engineering solution to a real data-quality problem in text editing.
Broad empirical coverage across an in-house benchmark, the public AnyText benchmark (English/Chinese), and handwritten datasets (IAM/CVL), with consistent quantitative gains over many baselines.
Ablations on the font style reference and text-region weighted loss weight λ are included and provide some insight into design trade-offs.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core technical contribution is largely an engineering combination of existing components (Qwen-Image-Edit backbone + LoRA, frozen VAE feature concatenation, a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL OCR model, and off-the-shelf DMD2 distillation). None of the sub-components are new, and the "dual-stream conditioning via concatenation" is a fairly standard trick that is not clearly differentiated from prior auxiliary-embedding/ControlNet approaches beyond parameter count.

The primary quantitative benchmark ("SkyReels-Text benchmark", 200 samples) is self-curated, not publicly released, and used for both main comparison and ablation, raising concerns about reproducibility and potential selection bias toward the proposed method's strengths.

Training data generation is partly circular: paired (original, edited) samples are produced using an unspecified "editing model" to swap text while preserving style, and the quality/realism of this synthetic supervision is not independently validated beyond automatic OCR/DINO checks — no human assessment of whether the generated pairs reflect genuine real-world font-background interactions.

No ablation or discussion of the distillation step (DMD2) despite it being listed as a contribution-adjacent component (8-step inference, 10x speedup); no speed/quality trade-off table is provided to substantiate the claim.

The ablation in Table 4 shows FSR actually hurts Sen.Acc/NED and GS on CVL is worse than DiffBrush, but these negative results are explained post hoc (blaming OCR evaluator limitations) rather than analyzed rigorously or acknowledged as a genuine limitation.

No explicit limitations or failure-case discussion anywhere in the paper, despite qualitative figures showing imperfect cases (e.g., Figure 4 rows with partial text corruption for competitors but no corresponding self-critical analysis for SkyReels-Text).

No user study or human perceptual evaluation despite the paper's central claims being about subjective typographic/style fidelity and "visual harmony," which automatic metrics (DINO, FID, LPIPS, B-PSNR) only partially capture.

Reproducibility is weak: no code, model, or dataset release is mentioned; compute budget (512 A100-hours) and proprietary baseline closed-source comparisons (Nano Banana, Seedream 4.0, FLUX-Kontext-Pro) make independent verification difficult.
The "Baseline" row in Table 2 is not clearly defined in the text (architecture/training details), making it hard to assess exactly what component the ablation in that table isolates.
Data provenance for the curated real-world poster dataset (design platforms, public repositories) raises potential copyright/licensing questions that are not addressed.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: font-controllable, reference-glyph-based text editing for professional poster/typographic design, which is under-served by both general-purpose editing models and existing specialized scene-text-editing methods.

The dual-stream conditioning design (reference-content poster + rendered glyph map, both encoded via a frozen VAE and concatenated along the sequence dimension) is simple, parameter-efficient, and avoids extra ControlNet/embedding modules, which is an elegant engineering choice.

The data curation pipeline with content-style decoupling (VLM-based OCR for detection, LLM-generated disjoint replacement text, and DINOv2-based style-preservation verification) is a thoughtful attempt to solve the content/style entanglement problem that plagues naive synthetic rendering pipelines.

Broad empirical evaluation across three distinct settings (in-house poster benchmark, AnyText English/Chinese benchmark, and zero-shot handwritten IAM/CVL benchmarks) with consistent, competitive-to-SOTA numbers against strong commercial (Nano Banana, Seedream 4.0, FLUX-Kontext-Pro) and open-source (FLUX-Text, AnyText2, TextCtrl) baselines.
Ablations on the font-style-reference conditioning and the text-region weighted loss hyperparameter λ are provided and give some insight into the accuracy/style trade-off.

Zero-shot generalization to handwritten text styles without any handwriting-specific training is a compelling demonstration of the method's flexibility, outperforming several dedicated handwriting-generation baselines on HWD.
weaknesses: The Font Style Reference ablation (Table 4) shows a large drop in Sen. Acc/NED when FSR is enabled (93.27%→83.34%), a non-trivial accuracy-style trade-off that is only briefly explained (blaming OCR evaluation limitations) rather than rigorously analyzed; this undercuts the claim of strong 'text fidelity' when font control is active.

The paper is largely built on top of an existing strong backbone (Qwen-Image-Edit) fine-tuned with LoRA plus a fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL OCR module; the core technical novelty (concatenating VAE features of two auxiliary images) is relatively lightweight engineering rather than a fundamentally new architecture, and this should be discussed more explicitly relative to prior glyph-conditioning works (FLUX-Text, TextFLUX).

The data-generation pipeline relies on an unspecified 'editing model' to produce style-preserving content-replaced training pairs; the identity/quality of this generator is not detailed, raising concerns about circularity (the final model's quality may be bounded by this intermediate generator) and about reproducibility.

No ablation isolates the contribution of the custom VLM-based OCR system versus standard OCR tools on final editing performance or downstream data quality, despite this being listed as a key contribution.

The primary in-house SkyReels-Text benchmark (200 samples) is self-curated and not released/described in enough detail (composition, licensing, selection criteria) for independent verification; comparator sets differ inconsistently between Table 1 (mostly generalist/commercial models plus FLUX-Text) and Table 2 (specialized text-editing methods), making it harder to assess relative standing comprehensively in one place.

No user study or subjective/perceptual evaluation of font-style fidelity is reported; DINO similarity and automated OCR-based metrics may not fully capture perceptual typographic quality, which is central to the paper's stated goal.

Practical costs (512 A100-hours for LoRA fine-tuning, 72 A100-hours for OCR fine-tuning, 100k curated samples) and reproducibility details (code/checkpoint release, exact backbone size, full inference speed benchmarks) are not discussed, limiting reproducibility for a paper emphasizing efficient, training-free inference for users.

Quantitative gains over the strongest baseline (FLUX-Text) on the AnyText benchmark are sometimes marginal (e.g., +1.37% Sen. Acc on English), so the 'state-of-the-art' framing should be tempered for some metrics even though FID/LPIPS improvements are more substantial.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and under-explored problem: font-controllable text editing for professional poster design, where users can supply arbitrary glyph patches instead of relying on font labels or classifier lists.

The dual-stream visual conditioning design (plain-text reference + glyph map, both encoded via a frozen VAE and injected alongside the noisy latent) is a clean, simple mechanism that avoids parameter-heavy ControlNet-style glyph embedding modules, and is well-motivated for decoupling content and style.

A carefully engineered data pipeline with content-style decoupling (VLM-OCR for detection, LLM-based divergent text generation, Nano Banana local editing, SAM2-based background transplantation, and dual verification via OCR NED and DINOv2 similarity) is a solid and reusable contribution beyond the model itself; the resulting 100K dataset and SkyReels-OCR-40K benchmark could be independently useful to the community.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning an in-house SkyReels-Text benchmark, AnyText (English/Chinese), and handwritten text (IAM/CVL) datasets, plus a user study against four commercial systems, provides fairly broad evidence of state-of-the-art performance across Sen. Acc., NED, FID, LPIPS, DINO, B-PSNR, and HWD metrics.
Ablations on the font-style-reference conditioning and text-region weighted loss are included and interpretable, giving some insight into which components drive gains.
Practical engineering contribution: an 8-step distillation (DMD2-based) for fast inference (~8s per edit) is reported, which matters for deployment in design tools.

Zero-shot generalization to handwritten text and multi-font editing in a single pass (without needing multiple rounds of interaction) is demonstrated qualitatively and is a differentiator versus prior text-editing methods that require separate fine-tuning per style/language.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is somewhat incremental: using rendered/glyph patches as visual conditioning for text style transfer has been explored (GlyphDraw, GlyphControl, DreamText, TextFLUX) and the architectural change here (concatenating VAE features of plain-text and glyph-map references with noisy latents in an MMDiT+LoRA backbone) is largely an engineering combination of existing ideas rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Most quantitative comparisons (Tables 1-3) are against the authors' own curated benchmark and pipeline-derived data, and the primary OCR model used for evaluation (Sen. Acc., NED) is the paper's own fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL OCR model, raising potential circularity/bias concerns since the same or a related model family is used both to build ground-truth text and to evaluate correctness.

The dataset construction and 'ground truth' generation pipeline itself relies on Nano Banana (a proprietary commercial model) for local editing and Qwen3-8B for divergent text generation; errors or biases in these components propagate into training data and benchmarks without independent human verification beyond automated NED/DINO thresholds, limiting the reliability of claimed 'high-quality' labels.

Reported metrics on the in-house benchmark (Table 1) show large jumps versus all baselines (e.g., Sen. Acc. 0.9334 vs. next-best 0.8266) that are difficult to fully trust given the benchmark and its scoring model were both designed by the authors; no external/human-annotated ground truth validation of the benchmark's difficulty or fairness (e.g., whether baselines were given equivalent conditioning information such as glyph patches) is discussed in detail.

The paper does not clearly state whether baseline methods (Nano Banana, Seedream 4.0, FLUX-Kontext-Pro, Qwen-Image-Edit) were given the same font/glyph reference input as SkyReels-Text; if these general-purpose editors were only prompted with text and not given the glyph patch, the comparison in Table 1/Figure 4 may be unfair since they lack the mechanism the paper claims is the key innovation.

Limitations are only partially and briefly acknowledged (e.g., paragraph-level editing challenges for artistic fonts, mentioned briefly in the supplementary); a dedicated limitations discussion is missing from the main paper, and there is no discussion of failure cases, sensitivity to poor-quality glyph patches, or performance under extreme font distortions.

Method description of the diffusion backbone, distillation and MMDiT training details is fairly terse (e.g., loss weighting choices, training schedule specifics, size/architecture of LoRA modules) — key hyperparameters are given but architectural specifics of the frozen 'MMDiT Block x N' are not elaborated, somewhat limiting reproducibility for those without access to the underlying Qwen-Image-Edit backbone.

The user study (Figure 7) lacks methodological details: number of participants, selection criteria, blinding procedure, and statistical significance testing are not reported, weakening the strength of the human-preference claims.

Some claimed contributions (e.g., 'simultaneous editing of multiple text regions... supporting complex multilingual layouts') are demonstrated only qualitatively (Figures 14-15) without corresponding quantitative multi-region/multi-font benchmark numbers.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem (fine-grained, font-controllable text editing for poster design) and proposes a clear formulation: using cropped glyph patches as explicit visual conditioning rather than font labels or text prompts, which avoids per-font fine-tuning.

The dual-stream conditioning (plain-text reference + glyph map, both VAE-encoded and concatenated with the noisy latent) combined with a text-region weighted reconstruction loss is a reasonable and simple architectural choice that is easy to understand.

Extensive empirical comparisons are provided against several strong commercial and open-source baselines (Nano Banana, Seedream 4.0, FLUX-Kontext-Pro, Qwen-Image-Edit, FLUX-Text, Calligrapher, AnyText family, handwriting generation baselines), together with ablations, a user preference study, and a large qualitative supplement.

The custom data-generation pipeline (content-style decoupling via LLM text replacement, editing, and dual verification with OCR/DINO) is a sensible engineering solution to a genuine data scarcity problem (lack of font-diverse, realistic text-image pairs).

Reported quantitative gains over baselines are large and consistent across multiple benchmarks (SkyReels-Text benchmark, AnyText, IAM/CVL), and the method generalizes zero-shot to handwritten text despite not being trained on handwriting data.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is a serious concern: the entire training data pipeline depends on closed, proprietary systems (Nano Banana/Gemini for local editing, Qwen3-8B for text replacement, a custom fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL OCR model), none of which are open or fully specified with hyperparameters/prompts. The main text-conditioning also depends on the closed Qwen-Image-Edit backbone. This makes the pipeline very difficult for others to reproduce even if code/weights for the LoRA adapter are eventually released.

The abstract states code and models are 'publicly available at' but no link, repository, or anonymized URL is actually given anywhere in the manuscript—this is either an oversight or indicates the release has not actually happened, undermining the reproducibility claim.

The benchmark used for the primary quantitative comparison (SkyReels-Text benchmark, 200 in-house curated samples) is created and curated entirely by the authors with their own OCR/DINO metrics, and the same organization's OCR model (fine-tuned Qwen2.5-VL) is used both to build the training/eval data and to score 'Sen. Acc'/'NED' for all competing methods. This creates a risk of metric/dataset bias favoring the proposed system, and the benchmark's composition, difficulty balance, and inter-annotator agreement (if any) are not described.

Technical novelty is incremental relative to cited prior work (GlyphDraw, GlyphControl, TextDiffuser, DreamText, FLUX-Text, TextFLUX): injecting glyph priors via VAE-encoded reference crops rather than embeddings/ControlNet is a reasonable but modest architectural change, and the paper does not clearly articulate why this specific design is superior beyond empirical results—no analysis of failure modes, computational cost of the extra VAE-encoded stream, or comparison against a matched glyph-embedding baseline under identical training data.
The user study methodology is under-specified (number of participants, instructions, selection criteria for the compared image sets), limiting the strength of the human-preference claims in Figure 7.

Figures throughout the paper (Fig. 1, 4, 14, 15) repeatedly render the brand name 'Skyreels'/'SkyReels' as example poster/font text, which both is a somewhat unusual/self-promotional choice for qualitative figures and raises a concern about identifying information being present in a purportedly blind-reviewed submission.

Ablation Table 4 conflates two different sweeps (FSR on/off, and λ values 0/1/2/5/10) in a way that is not clearly separated in the table structure, making it hard to verify which comparisons are apples-to-apples (e.g., is λ=5 with FSR on, and is the FSR ablation row using λ=5 by default?).

The paragraph-level editing extension (Section C, Fig. 13) is acknowledged by the authors themselves to be limited for non-standard fonts due to data scarcity, but this important limitation is only briefly mentioned in the supplementary material rather than discussed as a core limitation in the main paper.

Comparisons against commercial closed-source systems (Nano Banana, Seedream, GPT-4o family) are inherently less controlled (unknown training data, possible version drift, no access to internal parameters), which weakens the strength of head-to-head SOTA claims even though the direction of results is informative.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: fine-grained, font-controllable text editing for professional poster design, going beyond generic text replacement to control over typographic style via reference glyph patches.

Novel dual-stream visual conditioning design that decouples content (plain-text reference) and style (glyph map) via frozen VAE features, avoiding heavyweight glyph-embedding modules or ControlNet-style priors, and enabling zero-shot font transfer without font labels or test-time fine-tuning.

Careful data pipeline: a VLM-based OCR model fine-tuned for non-regular/calligraphic fonts, plus a content-style decoupling data generation pipeline (LLM-based divergent text generation, Nano Banana local editing, dual verification using OCR NED and DINOv2 feature similarity) that yields a 100K aligned pair dataset with quantitative diversity checks (t-SNE, NED/DINO distributions).
Text-region weighted loss is simple and well-motivated given the small area occupied by text regions in typical images, with an ablation demonstrating a sensible trade-off at lambda=5.

Extensive empirical validation: comparisons on an in-house SkyReels-Text benchmark, the public AnyText benchmark (English/Chinese), and handwritten text benchmarks (IAM/CVL), plus a user preference study against four commercial baselines (Nano Banana, Seedream 4.0, FLUX-Kontext-Pro, Qwen-Image-Edit) showing consistent wins.

Strong zero-shot generalization to handwritten text styles despite no dedicated handwritten training data, and to multi-font simultaneous editing within a single inference pass, which is a differentiator from methods requiring multiple rounds of interaction.
Reasonably thorough ablations (FSR on/off, lambda sweep) isolating the contribution of the two key architectural/loss components.

Supplementary material provides substantial additional detail (OCR dataset construction, content-style decoupling dataset pipeline, more qualitative examples including small-size and paragraph-level editing), aiding reproducibility of the data pipeline.
Includes a distillation step (DMD2-based) for practical 8-step fast inference, addressing a deployment concern relevant to poster-design workflows.
weaknesses: The overall pipeline depends on several proprietary/black-box components (Nano Banana for local editing/reference font generation, Qwen3-8B for divergent text generation, Qwen2.5-VL for OCR), which raises concerns about reproducibility for the community since these external models' behavior, availability, and versioning are outside the authors' control; the paper does not fully discuss how sensitive final results are to the quality/failure modes of these upstream models.

The dataset construction relies on automatic dual-verification (NED threshold 0.9, DINO threshold 0.8) rather than human verification at scale; only qualitative spot checks (Figure 11) and aggregate statistics are shown, leaving open the possibility of systematic content-style leakage or artifacts not caught by these thresholds.

The in-house SkyReels-Text benchmark (200 samples) used for headline comparisons and ablations is curated by the authors themselves, and comparison baselines (Nano Banana, Seedream 4.0, etc.) are commercial systems not fine-tuned for this specific task, which could bias comparisons in the proposed method's favor; no baseline that is retrained/fine-tuned on the same font-conditioning task is evaluated.

Paragraph-level and highly artistic/dense stylized text editing are acknowledged as limitations (paper explicitly states difficulty with paragraph-level artistic styles due to scarce training data), but this limitation is only briefly discussed, without deeper analysis of failure cases or an error taxonomy.

The text-region weighted loss and FSR conditioning are relatively incremental relative to prior glyph-conditioned text editing work (e.g., GlyphControl, TextDiffuser, FLUX-Text); the core novelty is more in the data pipeline and application framing than in fundamentally new architectural mechanisms, which may reduce perceived methodological novelty.

No explicit discussion of computational/training cost trade-offs relative to baselines (e.g., total GPU-hours for the OCR model, main model, and distillation) is given comparatively, other than absolute A100-hour figures, making it hard to assess efficiency claims relative to competitors.

Some quantitative comparisons (e.g., Table 1 on the in-house benchmark) do not report variance/confidence intervals or statistical significance testing, and the human preference study (Figure 7) lacks details on number of raters, inter-rater agreement, or evaluation protocol specifics.

The claim of "zero-shot" font transfer is somewhat weakened by the fact that the training data itself already spans a very large diversity of fonts (rich real-world poster fonts, calligraphic scripts, etc.); the boundary between "in-distribution generalization due to broad training coverage" versus true zero-shot transfer to unseen font families is not rigorously delineated.
